error_modes.label: Altitude control during the arrival and pattern entry

texts.0: SP, due to a descent rate that was never adjusted after the arrival was approved, did not level off at the assigned traffic pattern altitude. The altitude deviation exceeded 300 feet and the aircraft continued through pattern altitude toward the entry point. The IP took control to re-establish the aircraft at the published pattern altitude. SP did not stabilize the altitude at any stage of the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction in the descent toward the traffic pattern, allowed the deviation from the assigned pattern altitude to reach the 300 foot limit. SP began the correction only after the IP called the altitude, and the aircraft was returned to pattern altitude only after the pattern entry point had been passed. No control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted altimeter cross-check while setting up the arrival, allowed the altitude to deviate approximately 200 feet from the assigned traffic pattern altitude, between the 150 foot and the 300 foot limits. SP recognized the deviation without any prompting and re-established pattern altitude before reaching the entry point.
texts.3: SP flew the arrival with an accurate altitude cross-check and levelled off at the assigned traffic pattern altitude with deviations kept inside 150 feet. Corrections were small, promptly applied and completed before the entry point, so the aircraft was stabilized at pattern altitude throughout the entry.
texts.4: SP levelled off exactly at the assigned traffic pattern altitude and held it with negligible excursions, well inside 150 feet, throughout the descent, the entry and the initial leg. Power and pitch were coordinated so that the level-off required no visible correction.
texts.marginal: SP entered the traffic pattern within standards, but the altitude deviations were repeatedly close to the 150 foot value, all of them in the low sense, and each correction was applied only after the trend had developed. The tendency to descend below the assigned pattern altitude while the attention is on the entry geometry is expected to be removed by an earlier power adjustment and a more regular altimeter cross-check in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP returned the aircraft to pattern altitude with the deviation at about 280 feet before the entry point was reached. The late correction traced to the descent rate not being adjusted again after the arrival was first approved. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reconfirm the descent rate against pattern altitude continuously from the point of approval, not only once.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the deviation without prompting and re-established pattern altitude before the entry point, holding the excursion to about 210 feet. The interrupted crosscheck traced to the arrival set-up drawing attention away from the altimeter for longer than usual. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to interleave the altimeter crosscheck with the arrival set-up so it is not interrupted for an extended period.
texts_at.3: SP flew the arrival with an accurate altitude crosscheck and levelled off at the assigned pattern altitude with deviations kept inside about 95 feet. The small residual came from a correction applied a moment after the trend first appeared rather than at its onset. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the correction at the first indication of the trend rather than a moment after it appears.

texts_above.2: SP kept the altimeter crosscheck running through the arrival set-up and corrected the deviation before it grew, holding altitude to about 205 feet of the assigned value. Applying that correction at the very first indication of the trend, rather than a moment after, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control on the arrival.
texts_above.3: SP flew the arrival with an accurate altitude crosscheck and levelled off at the assigned traffic pattern altitude with deviations kept inside about 95 feet, corrections small and promptly applied. The technique is already sound; only the descent immediately after approval still calls for the crosscheck to be a shade tighter. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline on the arrival.
texts_above.4: SP levelled off exactly at the assigned traffic pattern altitude and held it with excursions inside about 30 feet throughout the descent, the entry and the initial leg. The only refinement available was to log the exact level-off point for the debrief, since altitude control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control through the pattern entry.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the arrival and pattern entry

texts.0: SP, due to an unplanned energy profile in which the descent was started with high power and no deceleration point, arrived at the pattern entry with an airspeed deviation of more than 20 knots from the briefed arrival speed. The aircraft could not be decelerated to the pattern airspeed before the entry point and the IP intervened on the power lever to recover the speed schedule.
texts.1: SP, due to a deceleration begun too late in the descent, reached the traffic pattern entry with an airspeed deviation at the 20 knot limit from the briefed arrival speed. The speed was brought back only after repeated verbal indications from the IP, and the aircraft was stabilized at pattern airspeed well after the entry point.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting that was not reduced when the descent angle increased, allowed the airspeed to deviate approximately 15 knots from the briefed arrival speed, between the 10 knot and the 20 knot limits. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator without prompting and re-established the pattern airspeed before the entry point.
texts.3: SP planned the deceleration so that the airspeed was held within 10 knots of the briefed arrival speed through the descent and the pattern entry. Power changes were anticipated and small, and the aircraft arrived at the entry point already at the pattern airspeed.
texts.4: SP flew the arrival on speed throughout, with airspeed excursions negligible and well inside 10 knots from the briefed value. The deceleration was planned early enough that the pattern airspeed was reached before the entry point without any late or large power correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed within standards, but the deviations remained close to the 10 knot value and were consistently in the fast sense at the pattern entry. The tendency to carry excess energy into the pattern is expected to be corrected by selecting an earlier deceleration point during the descent planning in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP brought the airspeed back to the pattern figure with the deviation at about 18 knots before the entry point was reached. The late deceleration traced to the point for slowing down being selected too far into the descent. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select the deceleration point earlier in the descent, before the airspeed has time to build up excess energy.
texts_at.2: SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator without prompting and re-established the pattern airspeed before the entry point, holding the deviation to about 14 knots. The late power reduction traced to the descent angle increasing without a matching adjustment of power. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reduce power as soon as the descent angle increases, not after the airspeed has already begun to build.
texts_at.3: SP planned the deceleration so airspeed was held within about 6 knots of the briefed arrival speed through the descent and the pattern entry. The small residual came from a power change applied a moment after the descent angle first increased. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the power change at the same moment the descent angle changes, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP reduced power as soon as the descent angle increased and identified the trend before it grew, holding airspeed to about 15 knots of the briefed arrival speed. Applying that power change at the same moment the descent angle changes, rather than a moment after, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control on the arrival.
texts_above.3: SP planned the deceleration so airspeed was held within about 6 knots of the briefed arrival speed through the descent and the pattern entry, with power changes anticipated and small. The technique is already sound; only the steepest descent angle still calls for the power change to be a shade quicker. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed energy management on the arrival.
texts_above.4: SP flew the arrival on speed throughout, with airspeed excursions negligible and well inside about 2 knots from the briefed value, deceleration planned early enough that pattern airspeed was reached before the entry point. The only refinement available was to log the deceleration point used for the debrief, since airspeed control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed control through the entry.

error_modes.label: Heading accuracy on the arrival and entry legs

texts.0: SP, due to a roll-out that was started without any reference to the target heading, exceeded 10 degrees of deviation from the required entry heading and continued to diverge from the traffic pattern axis. The aircraft was not aligned with the pattern leg and the IP took control to re-establish the correct heading before the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored roll-out rate at the end of the turn toward the field, stopped the turn with a heading deviation at the 10 degree limit from the required entry heading. The heading was corrected only after the IP pointed out the divergence, and the aircraft was aligned with the pattern leg late in the entry.
texts.2: SP, due to an anticipation of the roll-out that was not matched to the bank angle used, rolled out approximately 8 degrees off the required entry heading, between the 5 degree and the 10 degree limits. SP recognized the error immediately and corrected the heading with a prompt, measured turn before reaching the entry point.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the required entry heading with deviations kept inside 5 degrees and maintained it accurately along the arrival and entry legs. Roll-out was anticipated correctly for the bank angle used and no repeated heading corrections were needed.
texts.4: SP rolled out precisely on the required entry heading with negligible deviation and held the pattern axis exactly for the whole entry. The turn was planned with the correct lead point so the aircraft settled on heading without any subsequent correction.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the entry heading within standards, but the roll-outs were consistently close to the 5 degree value and always in the same direction, requiring a small further correction each time. The tendency to under-anticipate the roll-out is expected to be removed by using a fixed lead point related to the bank angle in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP corrected the heading onto the pattern axis with the deviation at about 9 degrees from the required entry heading before alignment was complete. The late correction traced to the roll-out rate not being monitored at the end of the turn toward the field. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to monitor the roll-out rate through the whole turn, not only at its very end.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error immediately and corrected the heading with a prompt, measured turn, holding the deviation to about 7 degrees from the required entry heading. The imprecise roll-out traced to the anticipation of the turn not being matched to the bank angle actually used. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to match the roll-out anticipation to the bank angle in use rather than to a fixed lead point.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out on the required entry heading with deviations kept inside about 3 degrees and maintained it accurately along the arrival and entry legs. The small residual came from a lead point set a touch early for the bank angle used on one turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to fine tune the lead point against the actual bank angle a little more closely on the next repetition.

texts_above.2: SP matched the roll-out anticipation to the bank angle actually used and corrected any residual with a prompt, measured turn, holding the deviation to about 6.5 degrees from the required entry heading. Fine tuning that anticipation against the actual bank angle from the outset, rather than adjusting it after roll-out, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid roll-out technique.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the required entry heading with deviations kept inside about 3 degrees and maintained it accurately along the arrival and entry legs, with roll-out anticipated correctly for the bank angle used. The technique is already sound; only the steepest turn toward the field still calls for the lead point to be sized a touch more precisely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate entry heading control.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out precisely on the required entry heading with negligible deviation and held the pattern axis exactly for the whole entry, the turn planned with the correct lead point so the aircraft settled without correction. The only refinement available was to log the lead point used for the debrief, since the roll-out itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding entry heading precision.

error_modes.label: Accuracy over the traffic pattern points and pattern geometry

texts.0: SP, due to an entry planned without identifying the traffic pattern reference points before the arrival, overflew the pattern points well outside the 0.5 NM maximum radius. The resulting ground track did not correspond to the published traffic pattern and the aircraft entered the pattern displaced from the correct leg. The IP took control to position the aircraft on the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a late visual acquisition of the airfield and its reference points, overflew the pattern points at the limit of the 0.5 NM maximum radius. The ground track was corrected toward the published pattern only after successive verbal indications from the IP, and the pattern geometry remained distorted for the first leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction that was not applied on the leg toward the field, drifted from the planned track and overflew a pattern point at a radius approaching but not exceeding 0.5 NM. SP identified the displacement against the ground references without prompting and re-established the correct pattern geometry on the following leg.
texts.3: SP identified the traffic pattern reference points early and overflew them within the 0.5 NM maximum radius, keeping the entry consistent with the published pattern. The legs were flown with correct wind correction and the resulting ground track reproduced the pattern geometry accurately.
texts.4: SP overflew every traffic pattern reference point with negligible displacement, well inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, and flew the entry geometry exactly as published. Wind correction was applied from the beginning of each leg so that the ground track required no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP flew the pattern entry within standards, but the overflight of the reference points was repeatedly close to the 0.5 NM radius and always on the outside of the published track. The tendency to widen the entry geometry is expected to be corrected by acquiring the reference points earlier and applying the wind correction from the start of the leg in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP corrected the ground track toward the published pattern with the overflight close to the 0.5 NM limit before the geometry was restored. The late correction traced to the airfield and its reference points being acquired visually later than the technique calls for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to acquire the airfield and its reference points earlier on the inbound leg, before the pattern geometry needs correcting.
texts_at.2: SP identified the displacement against the ground references without prompting and re-established the correct pattern geometry, holding the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. The drift traced to a wind correction that had not yet been applied on the leg toward the field. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply the wind correction from the start of the leg toward the field, not only once the drift is noticed.
texts_at.3: SP identified the traffic pattern reference points early and overflew them comfortably inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, keeping the entry consistent with the published pattern. The small residual came from a wind correction applied a moment after the leg toward the field began rather than at its start. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the wind correction at the exact start of the leg so no residual displacement remains.

texts_above.2: SP applied the wind correction from the start of the leg toward the field and identified any residual displacement without prompting, holding the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. Applying that correction at the exact start of every leg, rather than once a drift is noticed, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pattern geometry discipline.
texts_above.3: SP identified the traffic pattern reference points early and overflew them comfortably inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, with the legs flown with correct wind correction and the resulting ground track reproducing the pattern geometry accurately. The technique is already sound; only the leg toward the field still calls for the wind correction to be applied a shade earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pattern geometry accuracy.
texts_above.4: SP overflew every traffic pattern reference point with negligible displacement, well inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, and flew the entry geometry exactly as published from the beginning of each leg. The only refinement available was to log the wind correction applied on each leg for the debrief, since the geometry itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional pattern geometry precision.

error_modes.label: Descent planning and energy management for the arrival

texts.0: SP, due to workload management during the approach phase that left the descent planning undone until the field was in sight, arrived at the traffic pattern high and fast with no remaining distance to correct. The descent was flown with excessive rate and the aircraft was not established at pattern altitude and airspeed at the entry point. The IP took control to reposition the aircraft for a safe entry.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the arrival preparation into the last portion of the route, started the descent late and reached the entry point at the limit of the published altitude and airspeed values. The profile was retrieved only after repeated verbal direction from the IP on when to descend and when to decelerate.
texts.2: SP, due to an arrival plan that did not account for the tailwind on the inbound leg, began the descent slightly late and remained above the planned profile for part of the arrival. SP recognized the deviation from the planned descent point in time and adjusted power and rate to arrive at the pattern entry established at the correct altitude and airspeed.
texts.3: SP planned the descent point and the deceleration point before the arrival and flew the profile so that the aircraft was established at pattern altitude and pattern airspeed before the entry point. Power changes were anticipated and the arrival required no late corrections.
texts.4: SP calculated the descent and deceleration points accurately for the conditions of the day and flew the arrival with negligible deviation from the planned profile. The aircraft reached the traffic pattern entry fully established, with the workload of the arrival distributed evenly over the whole inbound leg.
texts.marginal: SP completed the arrival within standards, but the descent was consistently started later than planned and the profile was retrieved with rates and power changes larger than necessary. The tendency to compress the arrival workload into the final part of the route is expected to be corrected by fixing the descent and deceleration points earlier in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP established the aircraft at pattern altitude and airspeed with the altitude at about 275 feet and the airspeed at about 18 knots from the assigned values by the entry point. The late profile traced to the descent planning being left undone until the field was already in sight. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to plan the descent and deceleration points before the field comes into sight, on every arrival.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the deviation from the planned descent point in time and adjusted power and rate, establishing the entry with altitude at about 210 feet and airspeed at about 14 knots from the assigned values. The late start traced to the tailwind on the inbound leg not being accounted for in the arrival plan. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to account for the inbound wind when setting the descent point, rather than adjusting for it after the descent has begun.
texts_at.3: SP planned the descent point and the deceleration point before the arrival and flew the profile so the aircraft was established at pattern altitude and airspeed before the entry point, holding altitude to about 95 feet and airspeed to about 6 knots. The small residual came from a power change applied a moment after the plan called for it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the planned power change at the exact point called for, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP accounted for the inbound wind when setting the descent point and adjusted power and rate before a deviation could grow, establishing the entry with altitude to about 205 feet and airspeed to about 15 knots of the assigned values. Applying the planned power change at the exact point called for, on every arrival, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable descent planning.
texts_above.3: SP planned the descent point and the deceleration point before the arrival and flew the profile so the aircraft was established at pattern altitude and pattern airspeed before the entry point, holding altitude within about 95 feet and airspeed within about 6 knots. The technique is already sound; only a tailwind on the inbound leg still calls for the descent point to be adjusted a shade earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed energy management for the arrival.
texts_above.4: SP calculated the descent and deceleration points accurately for the conditions of the day and flew the arrival with negligible deviation from the planned profile, the workload distributed evenly over the whole inbound leg. The only refinement available was to log the computed points for the debrief, since the planning itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional arrival energy management.

error_modes.label: Safe entry: lookout, traffic sequencing and separation

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft position in the pattern, entered the traffic pattern without having established the position of the reported traffic and without a safe entry sequence. Separation from the preceding aircraft was not assured and the entry was not safe. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft outside the pattern before re-entering.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the traffic already established in the pattern, continued toward the entry point without adjusting the sequence and reached a spacing at the minimum acceptable value. The entry was made safe only after the IP directed both the extension of the leg and the visual search for the preceding aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to a lookout scan concentrated on the runway rather than on the pattern legs, acquired the preceding traffic later than required for a comfortable sequence. SP recognized the situation without prompting, adjusted the entry by extending the leg and re-established safe spacing before joining the pattern.
texts.3: SP maintained an effective visual lookout throughout the arrival, acquired the traffic in the pattern early and entered safely with correct sequencing and spacing. The position of the aircraft relative to the other pattern traffic was known at all times.
texts.4: SP built and maintained a complete picture of the pattern traffic from well before the arrival, acquired every reported aircraft visually and entered the traffic pattern with an unambiguously safe sequence and generous spacing. The lookout scan continued uninterrupted through the entry.
texts.marginal: SP entered the traffic pattern safely, but the traffic was acquired later than desirable and the spacing achieved, while acceptable, left little margin for a change of sequence. The tendency to concentrate the lookout on the runway rather than on the pattern legs is expected to be corrected by an earlier and wider visual search in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP extended the leg and re-established a safe entry sequence once the traffic was pointed out, though the spacing had reached the minimum acceptable value before the extension was made. The late adjustment traced to the traffic already established in the pattern not being tracked continuously from the earlier part of the arrival. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to track the pattern traffic continuously from the earlier part of the arrival, not only once it becomes close.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the situation without prompting, adjusted the entry by extending the leg and re-established safe spacing before joining the pattern. The late acquisition traced to the lookout scan being concentrated on the runway rather than on the pattern legs. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to include the pattern legs in the lookout scan from the start of the arrival, not only the runway.
texts_at.3: SP maintained an effective visual lookout throughout the arrival, acquired the traffic in the pattern early and entered safely with correct sequencing and spacing. The small residual came from a spacing check completed a moment after the traffic was acquired rather than at the same moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the spacing in the same moment the traffic is acquired, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP included the pattern legs in the lookout scan from the start of the arrival and adjusted the entry before spacing could tighten, re-establishing safe spacing well ahead of the pattern. Confirming spacing in the same moment traffic is acquired, on every arrival, would extend that margin still further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured traffic sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an effective visual lookout throughout the arrival, acquired the traffic in the pattern early and entered safely with correct sequencing and spacing, the position of the aircraft relative to other pattern traffic known at all times. The technique is already sound; only the earliest part of the arrival still calls for the pattern legs to be scanned a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate traffic sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP built and maintained a complete picture of the pattern traffic from well before the arrival, acquired every reported aircraft visually and entered with an unambiguously safe sequence and generous spacing. The only refinement available was to log the sequence used for the debrief, since the lookout itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional traffic awareness.

error_modes.label: Arrival checks, configuration and radio calls at the entry

texts.0: SP, due to workload distribution that left the SP flying and transmitting at the same time during the descent, did not complete the arrival checks and did not make the required call at the pattern entry point. The aircraft entered the traffic pattern in an incorrect configuration and without clearance from the tower. The IP intervened to complete the checks and to make the required transmission.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to shed a secondary task when the arrival workload increased, left the arrival checks unfinished until after the entry point and made the entry call late. The checks and the transmission were completed only after the IP prompted each of them; no control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption of the checklist by a radio exchange during the descent, omitted one item of the arrival checks at the point where it was required. SP detected the omission on the following check of the configuration and completed the item and the required call before the pattern entry point.
texts.3: SP completed the arrival checks at the planned points, configured the aircraft correctly for the pattern entry and made every required radio call in standard phraseology at the correct position. The cockpit workload was distributed so that flying the aircraft was never interrupted by the checks or the transmissions.
texts.4: SP sequenced the arrival checks, the configuration change and the radio calls so that each was completed early and without interference with the flight path. Every transmission was made in standard phraseology at the correct point and the read-back confirmed the actual clearance.
texts.marginal: SP completed all the arrival checks and calls within standards, but each was performed at the latest acceptable point and the transmissions were made while the aircraft was still being manoeuvred. The tendency to compress the checks and the radio work into the entry is expected to be corrected by starting the arrival checks earlier on the inbound leg in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP completed the arrival checks and made the entry call once both were prompted, though they had run to the limit of the available time before being finished. The late completion traced to a secondary task not being shed when the arrival workload increased. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to shed the secondary task as soon as the arrival workload increases, not only once the checks are already running late.
texts_at.2: SP detected the omission on the following check of the configuration and completed the item and the required call before the pattern entry point. The interruption traced to a radio exchange during the descent breaking into the checklist at the point where the item was required. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to resume the checklist at the exact item where a radio exchange interrupted it, rather than after the following check.
texts_at.3: SP completed the arrival checks at the planned points, configured the aircraft correctly for the pattern entry and made every required radio call in standard phraseology at the correct position. The small residual came from an item confirmed a moment after the radio exchange rather than immediately following it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to resume the checklist the instant a radio exchange ends, not a moment later.

texts_above.2: SP shed any secondary task as soon as the arrival workload increased and resumed the checklist at the exact item a radio exchange had interrupted, completing checks and calls before the pattern entry point. Resuming the checklist the instant the exchange ends, on every arrival, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady arrival check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP completed the arrival checks at the planned points, configured the aircraft correctly for the pattern entry and made every required radio call in standard phraseology at the correct position, the cockpit workload distributed so flying was never interrupted. The technique is already sound; only a radio exchange during the descent still calls for the checklist to resume a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed arrival check management.
texts_above.4: SP sequenced the arrival checks, the configuration change and the radio calls so each was completed early and without interference with the flight path, every transmission made in standard phraseology with the read-back confirming the actual clearance. The only refinement available was to log the sequence for the debrief, since the check management itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary arrival check management.

error_modes.label: Formation recovery and pattern entry discipline (N44XX / N45XX)

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate coordination with the formation lead during the recovery, did not fly the briefed formation arrival and did not hold the assigned position for the pattern entry. Spacing from the other aircraft was lost and the entry did not correspond to the briefed formation profile. The IP took control to restore separation and to re-establish the aircraft in the recovery pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to crew and formation coordination that did not survive the increase in workload at the recovery, held the assigned formation position only at the limit of the briefed tolerances during the descent and pattern entry. Position and spacing were restored after successive directions from the IP and from the formation lead, with corrections applied late.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed response to the lead power change during the recovery descent, allowed the formation position to open beyond the briefed spacing without exceeding the maximum. SP recognized the closure error and re-established the correct position and the briefed spacing before the pattern entry point.
texts.3: SP flew the formation recovery in the briefed position, responded promptly to the lead manoeuvres and entered the traffic pattern with correct spacing and sequence as briefed for the formation profile. Cross-talk with the other cockpit and with the lead was clear and timely.
texts.4: SP maintained the briefed formation position with negligible variation through the whole recovery, anticipated the lead manoeuvres and entered the traffic pattern with exact spacing and sequence. Coordination with the lead and within the cockpit was continuous and required no repetition.
texts.marginal: SP flew the formation recovery and pattern entry within the briefed tolerances, but the position corrections were consistently reactive and the spacing at the entry was at the wide end of the briefed range. The tendency to respond to the lead rather than to anticipate is expected to be corrected by closer monitoring of the lead attitude and power state in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP restored position and the briefed spacing once directed, though the correction had come only after successive directions from the IP and the formation lead. The late response traced to crew and formation coordination not surviving the increase in workload at the recovery. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the coordination with the lead active through the increase in workload at the recovery, not only before it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the closure error and re-established the correct position and the briefed spacing before the pattern entry point. The delayed response traced to the lead power change during the recovery descent not being answered immediately. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to respond to a lead power change during the recovery descent as soon as it is seen, not after the position has already opened.
texts_at.3: SP flew the formation recovery in the briefed position, responded promptly to the lead manoeuvres and entered the traffic pattern with correct spacing and sequence as briefed for the formation profile. The small residual came from a cross-talk exchange completed a moment after the lead manoeuvre rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the cross-talk exchange during the lead manoeuvre itself, not a moment after it.

texts_above.2: SP responded to the lead power change during the recovery descent as soon as it was seen, re-establishing position and the briefed spacing well ahead of the pattern entry point. Completing the cross-talk exchange during the lead manoeuvre itself, on every recovery, would tighten the margin still further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable formation coordination.
texts_above.3: SP flew the formation recovery in the briefed position, responded promptly to the lead manoeuvres and entered the traffic pattern with correct spacing and sequence as briefed for the formation profile, cross-talk with the other cockpit and with the lead clear and timely. The technique is already sound; only the busiest part of the recovery still calls for the response to be a shade quicker. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed formation coordination.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the briefed formation position with negligible variation through the whole recovery, anticipated the lead manoeuvres and entered the traffic pattern with exact spacing and sequence. The only refinement available was to log the anticipated manoeuvres for the debrief, since the coordination itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate formation recovery discipline.

error_modes.label: Radio calls at the proper location during the letdown and the actual location report

texts.0: SP, due to making the letdown and traffic entry calls at other than the proper location, reported positions the aircraft had not reached and never amended the report with the actual location. The controller sequenced the aircraft on a false position picture and SP, working the problem head down, left the published entry route with the heading more than 10 degrees off the inbound track. The IP took the radios, passed the actual location and turned the aircraft back onto the entry route.
texts.1: SP, due to transmitting the entry call short of the published reporting point, did not report the actual location of the aircraft as required when a call is made away from the proper location. Attention held on the radio allowed the track toward the entry point to open to the 10 degree limit before the IP verbally prompted both the corrected position report and the heading. The correct sequencing information reached the controller only at the limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a letdown call made before reaching the proper location, initially passed a reporting point the aircraft had not yet overflown. SP recognized the discrepancy without prompting, transmitted the actual location immediately and returned to the entry track with the heading no more than 8 degrees off. The remaining calls were made at the proper locations.
texts.3: SP made all letdown and traffic entry calls at the proper locations and, where one call could not be made exactly over the reporting point, reported the actual location of the aircraft. Heading toward the entry point stayed inside 5 degrees while transmitting. Radio work was integrated with the descent with no loss of aircraft control.
texts.4: SP transmitted every letdown and pattern entry call precisely at the proper location, with correct content, so the controller position picture matched the aircraft at all times. Heading and altitude excursions during the transmissions were negligible. No call required an actual location amendment because none was made away from its reporting point.
texts.marginal: SP made the required calls close to the proper locations and did report the actual location on the one call that slipped early, holding the heading just inside 5 degrees while transmitting. Radio and flying tasks were still handled one after the other, so every transmission produced a small track excursion. The tendency is expected to be removed by planning the calls against the published reporting points before the letdown in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP transmitted the corrected position report and heading with the deviation at about 9 degrees off the inbound track before the correction was complete. The late report traced to the entry call being made short of the published reporting point without an actual-location amendment. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to amend the report with the actual location every time a call is made away from the proper reporting point, from the first call of the letdown.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the discrepancy without prompting, transmitted the actual location immediately and returned to the entry track with the heading no more than about 7 degrees off. The premature call traced to the letdown call being made before the proper location had actually been reached. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm the aircraft has reached the reporting point before transmitting, rather than amending the report afterward.
texts_at.3: SP made all letdown and traffic entry calls at the proper locations and, where one could not be made exactly over the reporting point, reported the actual location, holding heading toward the entry point inside about 3 degrees. The small residual came from a heading correction applied a moment after the transmission rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the heading correction during the transmission itself, not a moment after it.

texts_above.2: SP confirmed the aircraft had reached the reporting point before transmitting and, where that was not possible, reported the actual location immediately, holding heading no more than about 6.5 degrees off the inbound track. Holding the heading correction during the transmission itself, on every call, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good radio and heading integration.
texts_above.3: SP made all letdown and traffic entry calls at the proper locations and, where one call could not be made exactly over the reporting point, reported the actual location of the aircraft, heading toward the entry point held inside about 3 degrees while transmitting. The technique is already sound; only a call slipping early still calls for the location amendment to follow a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed radio and heading integration.
texts_above.4: SP transmitted every letdown and pattern entry call precisely at the proper location, with correct content, so the controller position picture matched the aircraft at all times, heading and altitude excursions during the transmissions negligible. The only refinement available was to log the exact call timing for the debrief, since the radio work itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional radio discipline during the letdown.

error_modes.label: Surface winds assumed equal to the winds at pattern altitude

texts.0: SP, due to assuming that the surface winds passed by the tower were the same as the winds at pattern altitude, did not use the crab carried on the inbound leg or the GPS groundspeed at pattern altitude to estimate the pattern winds. The entry legs were flown with a drift correction taken from the surface report only, and the aircraft was displaced from the published track by well over 0.5 NM with the heading more than 10 degrees off the pattern axis. The IP took control to re-establish the aircraft on the pattern track.
texts.1: SP, due to carrying the surface wind report into the pattern without checking it against the drift correction required at pattern altitude, did not update the wind estimate before the entry. The uncorrected drift opened the entry heading to the 10 degree limit and the overflight of the pattern points reached the 0.5 NM radius. SP applied the correction only after the IP called the drift.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind estimate still based on the surface report, applied a drift correction that did not match the wind at pattern altitude. SP noticed the developing displacement on the entry leg without prompting, compared the GPS groundspeed with the indicated airspeed and re-established the track with the heading no more than 8 degrees off. The entry was completed on the published geometry.
texts.3: SP treated the surface winds as different from the winds at pattern altitude and estimated the pattern wind from the crab required and the GPS groundspeed at pattern altitude. The drift correction applied held the entry track with the heading inside 5 degrees and the pattern points overflown inside the 0.5 NM radius. No further wind adjustment was needed after the entry.
texts.4: SP established the wind at pattern altitude from the drift correction and the GPS groundspeed before the entry and flew the whole entry with that correction applied from the start of each leg. Heading held on the pattern axis with negligible deviation and the ground track matched the published pattern. The surface report was used only for the landing considerations.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated the crosswind control requirements and kept the entry inside standards, but the wind estimate was refined only after the first leg had already drifted, with heading corrections close to the 5 degree value. The tendency to start from the surface report and adjust late is expected to be corrected by checking the crab and the GPS groundspeed as soon as pattern altitude is reached in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP applied the drift correction called by the IP with the heading at about 9 degrees off the pattern axis and the overflight close to the 0.5 NM limit before the correction closed. The uncorrected drift traced to the surface wind report being carried into the pattern without a check against the drift required at pattern altitude. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the surface wind report against the drift required at pattern altitude before the entry, not only after the drift becomes visible.
texts_at.2: SP compared the GPS groundspeed with the indicated airspeed and re-established the track without prompting, holding heading no more than about 7 degrees off and the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. The developing displacement traced to the wind estimate still being based on the surface report rather than the pattern altitude drift. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compare GPS groundspeed with indicated airspeed as soon as pattern altitude is reached, not only once a displacement is noticed.
texts_at.3: SP treated the surface winds as different from the winds at pattern altitude and estimated the pattern wind from the crab required and the GPS groundspeed, holding heading inside about 3 degrees and the overflight comfortably inside the 0.5 NM radius. The small residual came from a wind adjustment made a moment after pattern altitude was reached rather than at that moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the wind adjustment at the exact moment pattern altitude is reached, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP compared GPS groundspeed with indicated airspeed as soon as pattern altitude was reached and applied the correction before a displacement could develop, holding heading no more than about 6.5 degrees off and the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. Making that comparison the instant pattern altitude is reached, on every entry, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid pattern wind estimation.
texts_above.3: SP treated the surface winds as different from the winds at pattern altitude and estimated the pattern wind from the crab required and the GPS groundspeed at pattern altitude, holding heading inside about 3 degrees and the pattern points overflown comfortably inside the 0.5 NM radius. The technique is already sound; only the moment pattern altitude is first reached still calls for the wind estimate to be refreshed a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate pattern wind estimation.
texts_above.4: SP established the wind at pattern altitude from the drift correction and the GPS groundspeed before the entry and flew the whole entry with that correction applied from the start of each leg, heading held on the pattern axis with negligible deviation. The only refinement available was to log the pattern wind established for the debrief, since the estimation itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding pattern wind estimation.

error_modes.label: Crosswind and headwind component estimation (60 to 1 rule, GPS groundspeed minus IAS)

texts.0: SP, due to not applying the 60 to 1 rule to convert the crab into a crosswind component and not taking the headwind as the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed, entered the pattern with no numerical picture of the wind. The descent was planned on the indicated airspeed alone, so the ground distance was misjudged, the entry legs were displaced beyond 0.5 NM from the pattern points and the aircraft arrived at the entry more than 300 feet from pattern altitude. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft for the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting the crosswind estimation from the drift correction carried, did not quantify the wind before committing to the entry. The unquantified tailwind component compressed the descent and the deviation from pattern altitude reached the 300 foot limit at the entry point. SP corrected the profile only after repeated verbal indications from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete crosswind computation in which the drift correction was noted but not converted with the 60 to 1 rule, planned the entry on an approximate wind. SP detected the error from the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed without prompting and adjusted the descent, keeping the altitude deviation near 200 feet and re-establishing pattern altitude before the entry point.
texts.3: SP converted the drift correction into a crosswind component with the 60 to 1 rule and took the headwind component as the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed. The wind figures obtained were used in the letdown plan, so the aircraft reached the entry point within 150 feet of pattern altitude and on the pattern track. Crosswind control requirements were anticipated for the pattern legs.
texts.4: SP computed the crosswind and headwind components before the letdown and refreshed them at pattern altitude, so the descent point and the entry geometry were based on actual groundspeed. Altitude and track at the entry point were held with negligible deviation. The anticipated crab matched the drift observed on every pattern leg.
texts.marginal: SP estimated the wind components correctly and stayed within standards, but the computation was made only once and was not refreshed at pattern altitude, so the last leg needed a correction close to the 150 foot value. The tendency to work from a single early wind figure is expected to be corrected by rechecking the GPS groundspeed against indicated airspeed at pattern altitude in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP corrected the profile with the deviation from pattern altitude at about 280 feet at the entry point before it was fully arrested. The compressed descent traced to the crosswind estimation being omitted from the drift correction carried into the arrival. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to quantify the crosswind and headwind components before committing to the entry, on every arrival.
texts_at.2: SP detected the error from the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed without prompting and adjusted the descent, keeping the deviation from pattern altitude near about 210 feet. The approximate wind traced to the drift correction being noted but not converted with the 60 to 1 rule. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to convert the noted drift correction with the 60 to 1 rule as soon as it is recorded, not later in the descent.
texts_at.3: SP converted the drift correction into a crosswind component with the 60 to 1 rule and took the headwind component as the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed, holding altitude within about 95 feet of pattern altitude at the entry point. The small residual came from the wind figures being applied a moment after they were computed rather than immediately. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the wind figures to the letdown plan the instant they are computed, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP converted the drift correction with the 60 to 1 rule as soon as it was recorded and used the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed for the headwind, holding altitude to about 205 feet of pattern altitude at the entry point. Applying the wind figures to the letdown plan the instant they are computed, on every arrival, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound crosswind and headwind estimation.
texts_above.3: SP converted the drift correction into a crosswind component with the 60 to 1 rule and took the headwind component as the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed, holding altitude within about 95 feet of pattern altitude and on the pattern track. The technique is already sound; only the busiest letdown still calls for the wind figures to be applied a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise wind component estimation.
texts_above.4: SP computed the crosswind and headwind components before the letdown and refreshed them at pattern altitude, so the descent point and the entry geometry were based on actual groundspeed, altitude and track held with negligible deviation. The only refinement available was to log the refreshed components for the debrief, since the estimation itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent crosswind and headwind estimation.

error_modes.label: Clearing turns during the VMC letdown

texts.0: SP, due to descending straight ahead in VMC without using clearing turns, did not clear the pattern entry route below and ahead of the aircraft and kept the attention inside the cockpit. The area under the nose was never checked, the descent rate was left unchecked and the aircraft passed through the traffic pattern altitude by more than 300 feet with unresolved conflicting traffic. The IP took control, cleared the area and re-established the aircraft above the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a letdown flown wings level with no clearing turn, did not obtain a view of the airspace masked by the nose and did not use the turn to control the descent rate. The uncontrolled rate brought the altitude deviation to the 300 foot limit at the level off and the pattern entry route was cleared only after the IP directed the turn. No control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a clearing turn started late and stopped short in the VMC letdown, did not complete the visual scan of the entry route and did not use the manoeuvre to steady the descent rate. SP recognized the omission without prompting, completed a second clearing turn and levelled off with the altitude deviation near 200 feet and the entry route clear.
texts.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown to clear the pattern entry route, to control the descent rate and to keep the attention on the outside visual references. The level off at pattern altitude was made inside 150 feet with the entry route confirmed clear. The turns were flown without disturbing the planned track to the entry point.
texts.4: SP planned and flew the clearing turns so that the whole entry route was covered visually, the descent rate stayed under control throughout and the outside references were used continuously. Level off at pattern altitude was achieved with negligible deviation and the track to the entry point was unaffected. Traffic in the pattern was acquired early as a result of the turns.
texts.marginal: SP flew the clearing turns and stayed within standards, but they were made after most of the descent had been completed and the rate corrections during them were close to the limit of what the profile allowed. The tendency to clear late in the letdown is expected to be corrected by starting the clearing turns at the top of the descent in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP cleared the pattern entry route with the deviation from pattern altitude at about 275 feet at the level off before the clearing turn was directed. The uncontrolled rate traced to the letdown being flown wings level with no clearing turn used to steady it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to use a clearing turn to control the descent rate from the first part of the letdown, not only once the rate has already built up.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the omission without prompting, completed a second clearing turn and levelled off with the deviation from pattern altitude near about 210 feet and the entry route clear. The incomplete scan traced to the first clearing turn being started late and stopped short in the VMC letdown. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the clearing turn earlier in the letdown so a second one is not needed to complete the scan.
texts_at.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown to clear the pattern entry route, to control the descent rate and to keep attention on the outside visual references, level off at pattern altitude made inside about 95 feet. The small residual came from a turn flown a moment later than the earliest point in the descent it could have started. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start the clearing turn a moment earlier in the descent so the residual altitude excursion is removed.

texts_above.2: SP started the clearing turn early in the letdown and used it to steady the descent rate before it could build up, holding the deviation from pattern altitude near about 205 feet with the entry route clear. Starting that turn a shade earlier still in the descent would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent clearing turn technique.
texts_above.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown to clear the pattern entry route, to control the descent rate and to keep attention on the outside visual references, level off at pattern altitude made inside about 95 feet with the entry route confirmed clear. The technique is already sound; only the earliest part of the descent still calls for the turn to start a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good clearing turn discipline.
texts_above.4: SP planned and flew the clearing turns so the whole entry route was covered visually, the descent rate stayed under control throughout and traffic in the pattern was acquired early as a result, level off achieved with negligible deviation. The only refinement available was to log the turn timing for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior clearing turn technique.

error_modes.label: Airfield information review before an arrival at a strange field

texts.0: SP, due to relying on prior familiarity instead of reviewing the airfield information before the arrival, did not have the airfield layout, the field elevation, the runway data or the tower frequency available at the alternate airfield. The pattern altitude was set from memory on wrong field elevation and the aircraft entered more than 300 feet from the correct pattern altitude and displaced from the published pattern. The IP took control, established the correct pattern altitude and completed the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to an airfield review left undone because the field had been visited before, did not confirm the runway data and the approach lighting for the arrival. The uncertainty at the entry point produced an altitude deviation at the 300 foot limit and a late identification of the landing runway, both resolved after verbal indications from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete review of the airfield information in which the frequencies were checked but the field elevation and runway data were not, entered the pattern with an approximate picture of the airfield. SP identified the discrepancy on the altimeter without prompting, corrected the pattern altitude within about 200 feet of deviation and completed the entry on the published geometry.
texts.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, field elevation, runway data, approach lighting, glide path guidance and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival, despite prior familiarity with the field. The pattern was entered at the correct altitude within 150 feet and on the published entry route. The required frequencies were selected before the entry point.
texts.4: SP reviewed the complete airfield information before the arrival and used it to build the entry plan, so pattern altitude, entry route and radio work were correct from the first call. Deviations at the entry were negligible and no item of airfield data had to be looked up after the letdown started. The arrival matched the training objectives briefed for the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP reviewed the airfield information and entered within standards, but the review was completed during the letdown rather than before it and one runway detail was confirmed only at the entry point, with the altitude deviation close to 150 feet. The tendency to rely on prior familiarity until the field is in sight is expected to be corrected by completing the airfield review before the descent in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP resolved the runway data and lighting uncertainty with the deviation from pattern altitude at about 275 feet at the entry point before it was fully corrected. The late resolution traced to the airfield review being left undone because the field had been visited before. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to complete the airfield review regardless of prior familiarity, before every arrival at a field not flown that sortie.
texts_at.2: SP identified the discrepancy on the altimeter without prompting, corrected the pattern altitude within about 210 feet of deviation and completed the entry on the published geometry. The approximate picture traced to the frequencies being checked but the field elevation and runway data left unreviewed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to review field elevation and runway data with the same priority given to the frequencies.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, field elevation, runway data, approach lighting, glide path guidance and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival, despite prior familiarity with the field, entry at the correct altitude within about 95 feet. The small residual came from a runway detail confirmed at the entry point rather than during the review. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm every runway detail during the pre-arrival review, not at the entry point.

texts_above.2: SP reviewed field elevation and runway data with the same priority given to the frequencies, identifying any discrepancy before the descent, holding the pattern altitude deviation within about 205 feet at the entry point. Confirming every runway detail during the review, on every arrival regardless of familiarity, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable airfield information review.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, field elevation, runway data, approach lighting, glide path guidance and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival, despite prior familiarity with the field, the pattern entered at the correct altitude within about 95 feet. The technique is already sound; only a field visited earlier that sortie still calls for the review to be a shade more thorough. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined airfield review technique.
texts_above.4: SP reviewed the complete airfield information before the arrival and used it to build the entry plan, so pattern altitude, entry route and radio work were correct from the first call, deviations at the entry negligible. The only refinement available was to log the review timing for the debrief, since the airfield information itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary airfield information discipline.

error_modes.label: Formation lead: low power settings below 20 percent torque in the recovery descent
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 1 and due to controlling the recovery descent with power settings well below 20 percent torque instead of using the speed brake, left Number 2 unable to hold position with the engine at idle. The formation accelerated through the planned descent profile and reached the pattern entry more than 20 knots off the briefed arrival speed with Number 2 out of position. The IP took control, restored the power setting and stabilized the descent.
texts.1: SP, flying as Number 1 and due to reducing power below 20 percent torque rather than extending the speed brake, gave Number 2 no power margin to correct with. The airspeed deviation at the entry reached the 20 knot limit and the power setting was restored only after the IP called for the speed brake. No control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, flying as Number 1 and due to a momentary power reduction toward the low end of the range during the descent, allowed the formation speed to deviate about 15 knots from the briefed arrival speed. SP recognized the low torque setting without prompting, restored the power above 20 percent and used the speed brake to hold the profile before the entry point.
texts.3: SP, flying as Number 1, avoided power settings below 20 percent torque throughout the recovery descent and used the speed brake to control the profile. The formation arrival speed was held within 10 knots of the briefed value and Number 2 retained a usable power margin for position corrections. The descent was delivered to the entry point on profile.
texts.4: SP, flying as Number 1, planned the descent so that the power stayed comfortably above 20 percent torque and the speed brake carried the profile adjustments. Airspeed excursions were negligible and Number 2 held position without large power changes. The formation arrived at the pattern entry exactly on the briefed speed and altitude.
texts.marginal: SP, flying as Number 1, kept the recovery descent within standards, but the power was allowed to approach the 20 percent torque value before the speed brake was selected, so Number 2 was left with a small margin on two occasions. The tendency to reduce power first and reach for the speed brake afterwards is expected to be corrected by selecting the speed brake as the primary drag device in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP, flying as Number 1, restored the power setting above 20 percent torque with the formation speed at about 18 knots off the briefed arrival value before the profile stabilized. The low setting traced to power being reduced below 20 percent rather than the speed brake being extended for the same effect. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select the speed brake as the first drag device, ahead of any power reduction below 20 percent, on every recovery.
texts_at.2: SP, flying as Number 1, recognized the low torque setting without prompting, restored the power above 20 percent and used the speed brake to hold the profile, keeping the formation speed to about 14 knots off the briefed arrival value. The momentary reduction traced to power being allowed toward the low end of the range before the speed brake was reached for. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reach for the speed brake before torque approaches the low end of the range, not after.
texts_at.3: SP, flying as Number 1, avoided power settings below 20 percent torque throughout the recovery descent and used the speed brake to control the profile, formation arrival speed held within about 6 knots of the briefed value. The small residual came from a speed brake adjustment applied a moment after the profile first needed it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the speed brake adjustment the instant the profile calls for it, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP, flying as Number 1, reached for the speed brake before torque approached the low end of the range, holding the formation speed to about 15 knots off the briefed arrival value with a usable power margin preserved for Number 2. Applying the speed brake the instant the profile calls for it, on every recovery, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady formation descent management.
texts_above.3: SP, flying as Number 1, avoided power settings below 20 percent torque throughout the recovery descent and used the speed brake to control the profile, the formation arrival speed held within about 6 knots of the briefed value and Number 2 retaining a usable power margin. The technique is already sound; only the steepest descent still calls for the speed brake to be reached for a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed formation descent management.
texts_above.4: SP, flying as Number 1, planned the descent so the power stayed comfortably above 20 percent torque and the speed brake carried the profile adjustments, airspeed excursions negligible and Number 2 holding position without large power changes. The only refinement available was to log the speed brake schedule for the debrief, since the descent management itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate formation descent management.

error_modes.label: Number 2 delay after the Break and spacing on downwind
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to starting the turn to downwind without waiting the minimum of 5 seconds after the Break of Number 1, produced insufficient spacing on downwind and closed on the lead aircraft. SP also rolled out inside the ground track of Number 1 instead of slightly outside it, so the interval for the landing sequence did not exist and the entry was not safe. The IP took control to re-establish spacing.
texts.1: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to a Break delay shorter than the minimum of 5 seconds, arrived on downwind with the spacing at the lower limit of what the pattern allows. SP extended the downwind only after the IP called the interval, and the position relative to the ground track of Number 1 was corrected late in the leg. No control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to a delay after the Break that was timed loosely rather than counted, started the turn slightly early and rolled out close to the ground track of Number 1. SP recognized the reduced spacing without prompting and adjusted the downwind position to sit slightly outside the lead ground track before the perch point.
texts.3: SP, flying as Number 2, waited the minimum of 5 seconds after the Break of Number 1 before starting the turn and rolled out on downwind slightly outside the ground track of the lead aircraft. The resulting spacing supported a normal contact pattern with the perch point unchanged. No adjustment to the interval was needed on the leg.
texts.4: SP, flying as Number 2, timed the delay after the Break precisely and established the downwind position slightly outside the lead ground track with the interval exactly as briefed. The pattern was flown as a normal contact pattern from the same perch point without any spacing correction. The landing sequence was assured from the roll out onto downwind.
texts.marginal: SP, flying as Number 2, respected the minimum delay after the Break and kept the spacing within acceptable limits, but the turn was consistently started at the earliest point of the delay and the downwind position sat only marginally outside the lead ground track. The tendency to close the interval is expected to be corrected by counting the delay deliberately and confirming the lead ground track before rolling out in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP, flying as Number 2, extended the downwind and corrected the position relative to the ground track of Number 1 once the interval was called. The short spacing traced to the delay after the Break being shorter than the minimum of 5 seconds. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to count the full 5 second minimum after every Break, not estimate it by feel.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the reduced spacing without prompting and adjusted the downwind position to sit slightly outside the lead ground track before the perch point. The early turn traced to the delay after the Break being timed loosely rather than counted precisely. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to count the delay after the Break deliberately rather than timing it by feel, on every recovery.
texts_at.3: SP waited the minimum of 5 seconds after the Break of Number 1 before starting the turn and rolled out on downwind slightly outside the ground track of the lead aircraft. The small residual came from the ground track confirmed a moment after roll-out rather than during the turn itself. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the lead ground track during the turn itself, not a moment after rolling out.

texts_above.2: SP counted the delay after the Break deliberately and rolled out slightly outside the lead ground track without needing a later correction, the resulting spacing supporting a normal contact pattern. Confirming the lead ground track during the turn itself, rather than after rolling out, would tighten the margin still further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable Break interval discipline.
texts_above.3: SP, flying as Number 2, waited the minimum of 5 seconds after the Break of Number 1 before starting the turn and rolled out on downwind slightly outside the ground track of the lead aircraft, the resulting spacing supporting a normal contact pattern with the perch point unchanged. texts.1: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to matching a pattern of the lead aircraft that was already outside normal parameters, did not fly a normal contact pattern of its own.
